summary:
What if you could become the commander of a mission to Mars?

Paws to Mars is an educational browser game for kids aged 7 to 12 that turns real NASA discoveries and missions into an interactive space adventure.
Players lead a crew of three animal astronauts, each with unique skills. Their mission is to manage the resources of a Martian base, explore the planet on rover expeditions, and complete investigations inspired by real places and events on Mars.

Along the way, they must face challenges, handle unexpected events, and make strategic decisions where every choice has consequences.
From Gale and Jezero craters to the 2018 global dust storm, the game turns scientific information into experiences that kids can discover and understand on their own.

Our goal is to bring space exploration closer to new generations, showing that learning science can also be an adventure.
In Paws to Mars, you don’t just learn about Mars: you become part of its exploration!
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

What does it take to keep a base running on Mars? How much energy should be set aside? What happens if radiation rises or a machine fails?

Paws to Mars invites kids aged 7 to 12 to find out by making them the heroes of a space mission.

It is a management and exploration video game that runs in the browser, developed with Godot 4.7. Players lead a crew of three astronauts and must keep a Martian base running. Each crew member has different skills and needs of their own, such as food, rest and health. Meanwhile, players must manage energy, oxygen and the systems that protect the base from radiation.

Exploration is also essential: players can send an astronaut out in the rover to investigate the planet. While that astronaut is away, players must keep managing the base with the resources and crew they have left. When the astronaut returns, new investigations can be unlocked.

In addition, critical events interrupt the mission routine and present situations with different options. Every decision has a cost and a consequence, forcing players to think strategically.

Why is NASA data important?

NASA science is the heart of Paws to Mars. We don’t use Mars simply as a backdrop: we build the adventure from places, discoveries and events related to real space missions.

Players explore a wide range of real missions and discoveries: the landing sites of rovers and probes such as Curiosity, Perseverance, Phoenix, Sojourner and the Viking missions; places like Gale Crater, Jezero Crater, Olympus Mons and Kasei Valles; the search for future base locations; the clues that ancient water left on the surface; and space weather. They also face events inspired by the history of Mars exploration.

One example is the global dust storm of 2018, which affected the Opportunity rover until its communications were interrupted, while Curiosity kept operating. This event becomes a challenge in the game: players must assess their resources and decide how to protect their own mission.

Every event includes references to its sources so that the information can be consulted and verified.

Our purpose is to turn scientific information that is usually found in technical documents and specialized reports into experiences that kids can understand, explore and remember.

What are the benefits and the expected impact?

Paws to Mars aims to bring space exploration closer to new generations, especially kids aged 7 to 12.

Through the game, participants can:

  • Develop strategic thinking by managing limited resources.
  • Understand how conditions on Mars affect space missions.
  • Learn about real discoveries and events in Mars exploration.
  • Practice problem-solving and decision-making.
  • Spark their curiosity about science, technology and space exploration.

We hope players will not only remember facts about Mars, but also understand why those discoveries matter and what challenges the people who study the planet face.

What makes our project creative?

Our proposal starts from a simple idea: what if kids could experience the difficulties of a space mission instead of just reading about them?

In Paws to Mars, scientific information becomes situations that require thinking and acting. A dust storm stops being just a historical event and becomes a problem the player must solve. Energy, oxygen and radiation stop being isolated concepts and have consequences within the adventure.

We also wanted to give the game its own identity through a crew of animal astronauts, inspired by the first animals that took part in space exploration. Their personalities and skills give every mission an element of strategy and teamwork.

Another important aspect is its visual identity: the characters, drawings, illustrations and backgrounds were made by hand by our team. We wanted to create a friendly, appealing visual universe that invites the youngest players to explore Mars.

Tools and technologies used

  • Godot 4.7: the engine used to develop the video game.
  • JSON: used to store the events and make it easy to add new scenarios.
  • Original art design: the characters, backgrounds, illustrations and visual elements were drawn and created by hand by the team.

What factors did we consider during development?

Our main starting point was the audience we wanted to reach: kids aged 7 to 12.

We know that scientific information about Mars can be complex, especially when it is presented through technical texts. That is why we aimed for an experience that is easy to understand without losing its educational value.

We took into account aspects such as:

  • Accessible language: short texts and simple words to explain scientific concepts and game mechanics.
  • Visual communication: warnings, colors and icons that make it easy to quickly recognize important situations, such as machine wear or the astronauts’ needs.
  • Progressive learning: a guided tutorial so that players can get familiar with the base and its resources.
  • Balance between fun and learning: the scientific investigations are part of the adventure and do not appear as separate lessons.
  • Scientific rigor: we used information from missions and official NASA sources to build the events and discoveries that inspire the game.

Our challenge was to find a way to bring real space exploration to the youngest players without losing the fun, curiosity and excitement of an adventure.
